content: An inorganic nonaqueous solvent is a solvent that is neither water nor an organic compound. Examples of such solvents include liquid ammonia, liquid sulfur dioxide, sulfuryl chloride, sulfuryl chloride fluoride, phosphoryl chloride, dinitrogen tetroxide, antimony trichloride, bromine pentafluoride, hydrogen fluoride, pure sulfuric acid, and other inorganic acids. These solvents are utilized in chemical research and industrial applications for reactions that cannot occur in aqueous solutions or require specific environmental conditions. In noble gas chemistry, reactions involving xenon-containing compounds are predominantly carried out in hydrogen fluoride or bromine pentafluoride. These solvents readily dissolve xenon difluorides and their derivatives. Occasionally, sulfuric solvents, such as sulfuryl chloride fluoride, are employed, particularly for reactions involving strong oxidants. Sulfuryl chloride fluoride is the preferred solvent for many reactions involving extreme oxidants. For instance, it is used to generate and study free carbocations and arenium ions. Acid-base reactions in nonaqueous solvents are typically described using the solvent-system definition. However, the Brønsted-Lowry theory can also be applied to protic solvents, which contain a dissociable hydrogen atom. According to the solvent-system definition, acids are compounds that increase the concentration of solvated positive ions (solvonium ions), while bases increase the concentration of solvated negative ions (solvate ions). These ions are in equilibrium with the neutral molecules of the pure solvent. For example, in liquid ammonia, sodium amide (NaNH₂) acts as a base, and ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) acts as an acid. Their reaction produces a salt and regenerates the solvent. The limiting acid in a given solvent is the solvonium ion, such as the hydronium ion (H₃O⁺) in water. An acid stronger than the limiting acid will exist predominantly in its dissociated form in that solvent. Similarly, the limiting base is the solvate ion, such as the hydroxide ion (OH⁻) in water. A base stronger than the limiting base cannot exist in solution, as it will react with the solvent. For example, in liquid ammonia, the limiting base is the amide ion (NH₂⁻), which is a stronger base than the hydroxide ion and cannot exist in aqueous solution. Acids stronger than the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) will act as strong acids in liquid ammonia. Acetic acid, for instance, is completely dissociated in liquid ammonia. Adding pure acetic acid or ammonium acetate to a liquid ammonia solution has the same effect on its acidity, though the latter is preferred for safety reasons. Bases that cannot exist in aqueous solutions can exist in liquid ammonia. This includes bases stronger than the hydroxide ion but weaker than the amide ion. Many carbon anions can be formed in liquid ammonia through the action of the amide ion on organic molecules, as seen with sodium amide. On the other end of the spectrum, superacids are media in which the hydrogen ion is only weakly solvated. A classic example is a mixture of antimony pentafluoride and liquid hydrogen fluoride. In this mixture, the limiting base, the hexafluoroantimonate anion (SbF₆⁻), is so weakly attracted to the hydrogen ion that virtually any other base will bind more strongly. This property allows the mixture to protonate organic molecules that would not be considered bases in other solvents. Comparing acidity and basicity between solvents is complex. While there is extensive data on acid strengths in aqueous solutions (pKa values), transferring this information to other solvents is challenging. Such comparisons often overlook the effects of solvation on the stability of other species involved in the equilibrium. Gas-phase acidities (proton affinities) can be measured, but their relative order often differs significantly from aqueous acidities. Few quantitative studies on acidities in nonaqueous solvents exist, though some qualitative data are available. Acids with a pKa value of less than 9 in water are generally strong acids in liquid ammonia. It is important to note that pH values are undefined in aprotic solvents, as the definition of pH assumes the presence of hydronium ions. In other solvents, the concentration of the respective solvonium or solvate ions should be used, such as pCl in phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃).
